--- title: "How to develop and submit a package to Bioconductor" subtitle: "Bioconductor Africa Seminar series" author: "Fabrício Almeida-Silva, Ph.D" date: "2026-10-28" description: | This session will introduce biologists and bioinformaticians to the process of developing and submitting a package to Bioconductor. We will cover the key steps involved in building a Bioconductor package, from structuring and documenting R code to testing, checking, and preparing a package for submission. categories: [Bioconductor, R, package development] format: revealjs: footer: "@almeidasilvaf | BioCAfrica: Bioconductor package development" --- ## About me :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="65%"} - PhD Bioinformatics (Ghent University), currently FWO-funded postdoc - Active contributor to the Bioconductor project: - 10+ contributed packages - Community Advisory Board (CAB) - Training Committee - Package reviewer - Research interests: network biology, evolution, gene regulation. ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ![](../../assets/images/photo.jpg){width="100%"} ::: :::: ## Outline 1. **Before you write code**: scope, package types, design principles, tools 2. **Anatomy of a package**: going through it one file or folder at a time 3. **Checking and submitting**: `R CMD check`, `BiocCheck`, the review process 4. **Maintaining a package** after it's been accepted
::: {.keybox} 📖 The main reference for everything in this talk is the [Bioconductor Contributions Guide](https://contributions.bioconductor.org/). For general R package development, see [*R Packages* (2e)](https://r-pkgs.org/) by Hadley Wickham & Jennifer Bryan. ::: # Before you write code {background-color="#1a81c2"} ## What is Bioconductor? - A repository of **open-source R packages** for analysing and understanding **high-throughput biological data** - \> 2,300 software packages, plus annotation and experiment data packages - Two releases per year (~April and ~October), each tied to an R version - A **community**: developers, reviewers, support site, Zulip chat, conferences
. . . Packages are **reviewed before acceptance** and **built and checked nightly** on Linux, macOS and Windows. ## Is my package in scope? Bioconductor packages should address the analysis of **high-throughput biological data**: sequencing, microarrays, flow cytometry, mass spectrometry, imaging, single-cell, etc. . . .
Core principles: - **Interoperability**: reuse Bioconductor data structures and infrastructure - **Best practices**: complete documentation, executed vignettes, unit tests - **Commitment** to maintaining the package and answering user questions ## Scope is described with **biocViews** *biocViews* are terms from a controlled vocabulary that classify packages. They're shown on the landing page and are used for searching. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} views <- read.dcf( url("https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/VIEWS"), fields = c("Package", "biocViews") ) pkgs <- c("DESeq2", "scater") v <- views[views[, "Package"] %in% pkgs, ] for (i in seq_len(nrow(v))) { cat(v[i, "Package"], ":\n", sep = "") cat(strwrap(gsub("\n", " ", v[i, "biocViews"]), indent = 4, exdent = 4, width = 75), sep = "\n") } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` DESeq2: Sequencing, RNASeq, ChIPSeq, GeneExpression, Transcription, Normalization, DifferentialExpression, Bayesian, Regression, PrincipalComponent, Clustering, ImmunoOncology scater: ImmunoOncology, SingleCell, RNASeq, QualityControl, Preprocessing, Normalization, Visualization, DimensionReduction, Transcriptomics, GeneExpression, Sequencing, Software, DataImport, DataRepresentation, Infrastructure, Coverage ``` ::: ::: ## Choosing biocViews - Browse the hierarchy at [bioconductor.org/packages/release/BiocViews.html](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/BiocViews.html) - Pick **at least two leaf terms** (the most specific ones) from the same trunk - Terms are **case-sensitive**, and must be on a single comma-separated line ```default biocViews: Software, Transcriptomics, RNASeq, Normalization, GeneExpression ``` . . .
::: {.keybox} 💡 Look at the biocViews of packages similar to yours. You'll often find terms you hadn't thought of. ::: ## Types of Bioconductor packages | Type | What it contains | Example | |------|------------------|---------| | **Software** | Algorithms, data access, visualisation (most packages) | `DESeq2`, `scater` | | **Annotation** | Database-like packages that map IDs to other information | `org.Hs.eg.db` | | **Experiment data** | Data sets to illustrate analyses and methods | `airway` | | **Workflow** | Long-form vignettes showing multi-package analyses | `rnaseqGene` | : {tbl-colwidths="[20,55,25]"}
::: {.muted} For large data, consider [AnnotationHub](https://bioconductor.org/packages/AnnotationHub) and [ExperimentHub](https://bioconductor.org/packages/ExperimentHub) instead of packaging the data. There are also [Bioconductor books](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/). ::: ## What makes a good package? :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Integration with the ecosystem** - **Interoperability**: take and return Bioconductor classes - **Don't reinvent the wheel**: reuse existing import functions, classes and methods - **Lightweight**: as few dependencies as possible - **Tested and documented** ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Small, focused functions** - Each function does **one thing** (split anything longer than a screen) - A **consistent API**: similar argument names across functions, `camelCase` or `snake_case`. - Few exported functions that users actually need; helpers stay internal (`.helperName()`) ::: :::: ## Interoperability: reuse Bioconductor classes ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| fig-width: 10 flowchart LR A[Raw data
FASTQ, BAM, counts] --> B["Import
(rtracklayer, tximport, ...)"] B --> C(["SummarizedExperiment
SingleCellExperiment
GRanges"]) C --> D[Your package] D --> C C --> E["Other packages
(DESeq2, scater, ...)"] style C fill:#87b13f,color:#fff style D fill:#1a81c2,color:#fff ``` ## Tools that make development easier | Package | Functionality | |---------|-------------------| | [usethis](https://usethis.r-lib.org/) | Creating packages and files: `create_package()`, `use_r()`, `use_test()`, `use_vignette()` | | [devtools](https://devtools.r-lib.org/) | Development cycle: `load_all()`, `document()`, `test()`, `check()` | | [roxygen2](https://roxygen2.r-lib.org/) | Writing documentation and `NAMESPACE` from comments in R code | | [testthat](https://testthat.r-lib.org/) + [covr](https://covr.r-lib.org/) | Unit tests and test coverage | | [biocthis](https://bioconductor.org/packages/biocthis) | Bioconductor-flavoured templates: `use_bioc_description()`, `use_bioc_vignette()`, `use_bioc_github_action()` | | [BiocCheck](https://bioconductor.org/packages/BiocCheck) | Bioconductor-specific checks before submission | : {.smaller tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"} ## A typical development workflow ```r # Step 1: Create the skeleton of a new package usethis::create_package("~/Documents/toyBioc") # Step 2: Add Bioconductor-style files with biocthis biocthis::use_bioc_description() # DESCRIPTION with biocViews etc. biocthis::use_bioc_vignette("toyBioc") # vignette template with BiocStyle biocthis::use_bioc_github_action() # GitHub Actions to check the package ## Step 3: Write code and tests usethis::use_r("normalizeCounts") # creates R/normalizeCounts.R usethis::use_test("normalizeCounts") # creates tests/testthat/test-normalizeCounts.R ## The development loop: repeat until happy devtools::load_all() # load the package (like library()) devtools::document() # update man/ and NAMESPACE devtools::test() # run unit tests devtools::check() # run R CMD check ``` # Anatomy of a package {background-color="#1a81c2"} ## Package structure ```{=html} 
toyBioc/├── DESCRIPTION├── NAMESPACE├── NEWS.md├── README.md├── R/├── man/├── tests/│   ├── testthat.R│   └── testthat/├── src/  (optional)├── data/├── inst/│   ├── extdata/│   └── scripts/└── vignettes/
  • DESCRIPTION: metadata
  • NAMESPACE: what's imported and exported
  • R/: R code
  • man/: documentation (generated by roxygen2)
  • tests/: unit tests
  • src/: compiled code (C/C++, Rust), optional
  • data/: R objects (.rda) for examples
  • inst/: files installed as they are
  • vignettes/: long-form documentation
  • README.md, NEWS.md: other files
``` ## Package structure: DESCRIPTION {.anatomy-slide} ```{=html} 
toyBioc/├── DESCRIPTION├── NAMESPACE├── NEWS.md├── README.md├── R/├── man/├── tests/│   ├── testthat.R│   └── testthat/├── src/  (optional)├── data/├── inst/│   ├── extdata/│   └── scripts/└── vignettes/
  • DESCRIPTION: metadata
  • NAMESPACE: what's imported and exported
  • R/: R code
  • man/: documentation (generated by roxygen2)
  • tests/: unit tests
  • src/: compiled code (C/C++, Rust), optional
  • data/: R objects (.rda) for examples
  • inst/: files installed as they are
  • vignettes/: long-form documentation
  • README.md, NEWS.md: other files
``` ## DESCRIPTION ```default Package: toyBioc Title: Normalization of RNA-seq Count Matrices Version: 0.99.0 Authors@R: person("Fabrício", "Almeida-Silva", email = "fabricio@example.com", role = c("aut", "cre"), comment = c(ORCID = "0000-0000-0000-0000")) Description: toyBioc provides functions to normalize RNA-seq count data stored in matrices and SummarizedExperiment objects. It implements counts per million (CPM) and log-transformed CPM. It also provides diagnostic plots to compare samples before and after normalization. License: GPL-3 URL: https://github.com/username/toyBioc BugReports: https://github.com/username/toyBioc/issues biocViews: Software, Transcriptomics, RNASeq, Normalization Imports: SummarizedExperiment, methods, stats Suggests: BiocStyle, knitr, rmarkdown, testthat (>= 3.0.0), ggplot2 VignetteBuilder: knitr ``` New packages start at version **0.99.0**. There's exactly **one maintainer** (`cre`), with an email address you actively read. ## DESCRIPTION: advertise your package The `Description` field is shown at the top of your package's **landing page**. It's often the first thing potential users read. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.bad} ```default Description: Normalize data. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.good} ```default Description: toyBioc provides functions to normalize RNA-seq count data stored in matrices and SummarizedExperiment objects. It implements counts per million (CPM) and log-transformed CPM, and provides diagnostic plots to compare samples before and after normalization. ``` ::: ::: :::: - At least **3 complete sentences**: what does it do, for which data, and why should I use it? - A **brief but descriptive** `Title` ## DESCRIPTION: Depends, Imports, Suggests | Field | Used for | | |-------|-----------|-| | `Imports` | Packages whose functions or classes your code uses | Most packages go here | | `Suggests` | Packages used only in vignettes, examples, tests, or optional code | `knitr`, `testthat`, `BiocStyle` | | `Depends` | Packages users *always* need attached with yours (e.g., infrastructure pkgs) | Rarely needed; more than 3 is unusual | : {tbl-colwidths="[18,50,32]"}
- Each package should appear in **only one** of these fields - **Bioconductor packages in `Imports`**: interoperability ## Mind the number of dependencies Dependencies can break and/or make package installation slower. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} deps <- tools::package_dependencies( c("S4Vectors", "SummarizedExperiment"), db = installed.packages(), recursive = TRUE ) lengths(deps) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> S4Vectors SummarizedExperiment #> 8 24 ``` ::: ::: . . . Before adding a dependency, ask yourself: - Do I need the whole package for **one small function**? - Is the function used in the **core** of my package, or in a niche feature? ## Move niche dependencies to Suggests A heavy package used only in one rarely-used function can go to `Suggests`. ```r plotDensities <- function(se) { if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) { stop("Package 'ggplot2' is required for this function. ", "Install it with BiocManager::install('ggplot2').") } df <- .longFormat(se) ggplot2::ggplot(df, ggplot2::aes(x = value, colour = sample)) + ggplot2::geom_density() } ```
::: {.keybox} 💡 Use `pkg::fun()` for packages in `Suggests`. Don't import them in `NAMESPACE`. ::: ## DESCRIPTION: License - Bioconductor packages must be **open-source**: use a standard license and give its version - `GPL-3`, `GPL-2`, `Artistic-2.0` (common in core packages), `MIT + file LICENSE`, ... - Licenses that **restrict use** are **not suitable**: - `CC BY-NC 4.0`, `CC BY-NC-SA 4.0`, `CC BY-NC-ND 4.0` (no commercial use), `ACM` - Check that your license is compatible with the licenses of your dependencies (and of any third-party code you include) ## Package structure: NAMESPACE {.anatomy-slide} ```{=html} 
toyBioc/├── DESCRIPTION├── NAMESPACE├── NEWS.md├── README.md├── R/├── man/├── tests/│   ├── testthat.R│   └── testthat/├── src/  (optional)├── data/├── inst/│   ├── extdata/│   └── scripts/└── vignettes/
  • DESCRIPTION: metadata
  • NAMESPACE: what's imported and exported
  • R/: R code
  • man/: documentation (generated by roxygen2)
  • tests/: unit tests
  • src/: compiled code (C/C++, Rust), optional
  • data/: R objects (.rda) for examples
  • inst/: files installed as they are
  • vignettes/: long-form documentation
  • README.md, NEWS.md: other files
``` ## NAMESPACE List of **imports** and **exports** created automatically by {roxygen2} from `@export` and `@importFrom` tags. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.bad} ```r #' @import SummarizedExperiment #' @import ggplot2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.good} ```r #' @importFrom SummarizedExperiment assay #' @importFrom stats median ``` ::: ::: :::: Running `devtools::document()` creates the NAMESPACE file: ```default # Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand export(normalizeCounts) importFrom(SummarizedExperiment,assay) importFrom(stats,median) ``` ## Package structure: R/ and man/ {.anatomy-slide} ```{=html} 
toyBioc/├── DESCRIPTION├── NAMESPACE├── NEWS.md├── README.md├── R/├── man/├── tests/│   ├── testthat.R│   └── testthat/├── src/  (optional)├── data/├── inst/│   ├── extdata/│   └── scripts/└── vignettes/
  • DESCRIPTION: metadata
  • NAMESPACE: what's imported and exported
  • R/: R code
  • man/: documentation (generated by roxygen2)
  • tests/: unit tests
  • src/: compiled code (C/C++, Rust), optional
  • data/: R objects (.rda) for examples
  • inst/: files installed as they are
  • vignettes/: long-form documentation
  • README.md, NEWS.md: other files
``` ## R/: what a function looks like ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r normalizeCounts <- function(counts, method = c("cpm", "log2cpm")) { method <- match.arg(method) .checkCounts(counts) libsize <- colSums(counts) cpm <- t(t(counts) / libsize) * 1e6 if (method == "log2cpm") { cpm <- log2(cpm + 1) } return(cpm) } ``` ::: ::: - **Validate inputs** early (here, in the internal helper `.checkCounts()`) - 4 spaces of indentation, ≤ 80 characters per line, `<-` for assignment ## R/: documenting functions with roxygen2 ```r #' Normalize a matrix of RNA-seq counts #' #' @param counts A numeric matrix of raw read counts, with genes in rows #' and samples in columns. #' @param method Character indicating the normalization method. One of #' "cpm" (counts per million) or "log2cpm" (log2 of CPM + 1). #' Default: "cpm". #' #' @return A numeric matrix with the same dimensions as `counts`, #' containing normalized expression values. #' #' @export #' #' @examples #' counts <- matrix(c(10, 0, 5, 20, 3, 7), nrow = 3) #' normalizeCounts(counts, method = "log2cpm") normalizeCounts <- function(counts, method = c("cpm", "log2cpm")) { ``` `devtools::document()` creates `man/normalizeCounts.Rd` and updates `NAMESPACE`. **Every exported** function needs a man page with **runnable examples** ## Docs: say what each parameter *is* :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.bad} ```r #' @param counts Counts. #' @param method Method to use. #' @param min_count Minimum count. #' @param plot Whether to plot or not. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.good} ```r #' @param counts A numeric matrix of raw #' read counts, with genes in rows and #' samples in columns. #' @param method Character indicating the #' normalization method. One of "cpm" or #' "log2cpm". Default: "cpm". #' @param min_count Numeric scalar indicating #' the minimum count for a gene to be kept. #' Default: 10. #' @param plot Logical indicating whether to #' plot densities. Default: FALSE. ``` ::: ::: :::: State the **class** (numeric, character, logical, `SummarizedExperiment`, ...), the **expected shape** (scalar, vector, matrix), the **valid values**, and the **default**. ## Docs: describe what's returned :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.bad} ```r #' @return A data frame with #' the results. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.good} ```r #' @return A data frame with the #' following columns: #' \describe{ #' \item{gene}{Character, gene ID.} #' \item{logFC}{Numeric, log2 fold #' change (treatment vs control).} #' \item{pvalue}{Numeric, P-value.} #' \item{padj}{Numeric, P-value adjusted #' for multiple testing (BH method).} #' \item{significant}{Logical, whether #' `padj` < `alpha`.} #' } ``` ::: ::: :::: When a function returns a data frame (or a list), document **every column (or element)** and its **type**. ## Code: some do's and don'ts :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.bad} ```r # Bad 1: if `x` is empty lapply(1:length(x), ...) # Bad 2: type not explicit res <- sapply(x, mean) # Bad 3: 2+ classes, inheritance if(class(se) == "SummarizedExperiment") # Bad 4: `T` can be a variable normalizeCounts(counts, log = T) # Bad 5: `cat()` cannot be silenced cat("Normalizing", n, "samples...\n") # Bad 6: `set.seed()` inside code set.seed(123) idx <- sample(ncol(counts), 10) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.good} ```r # Good 1: empty sequence with empty `x` lapply(seq_along(x), ...) # Good 2: explicit type res <- vapply(x, mean, numeric(1)) # Good 3: inheritance handled if(is(se, "SummarizedExperiment")) # Good 4: `TRUE` or `FALSE normalizeCounts(counts, log = TRUE) # Good 5: `message()`/`warning()`/`stop()` message("Normalizing ", n, " samples...") # Good 6: let users set the seed idx <- sample(ncol(counts), 10) ``` ::: ::: :::: See the full list [here](https://contributions.bioconductor.org/r-code.html#r-code-best-practices-and-guidelines). ## R/: S4 classes, a short example Before creating a new class, check whether an existing one can hold your data (or be **extended**). If you do need one: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} setClass("CountSet", slots = c(counts = "matrix", condition = "factor"), validity = function(object) { if (ncol(object@counts) != length(object@condition)) return("ncol(counts) must equal length(condition)") TRUE } ) ## A constructor (users never call new() directly) CountSet <- function(counts, condition) { new("CountSet", counts = counts, condition = factor(condition)) } ``` ::: ## R/: S4 generics, methods and show() ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} setGeneric("counts", function(object) standardGeneric("counts")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "counts" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} setMethod("counts", "CountSet", function(object) object@counts) setMethod("show", "CountSet", function(object) { cat("CountSet with", nrow(object@counts), "genes and", ncol(object@counts), "samples\n") cat("Conditions:", levels(object@condition), "\n") }) cs <- CountSet(matrix(rpois(20, 10), nrow = 5), rep(c("ctrl", "trt"), 2)) cs ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> CountSet with 5 genes and 4 samples #> Conditions: ctrl trt ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} CountSet(matrix(rpois(20, 10), nrow = 5), c("ctrl", "trt")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` #> Error in `validObject()`: #> ! invalid class "CountSet" object: ncol(counts) must equal length(condition) ``` ::: ::: ## Package structure: tests/ {.anatomy-slide} ```{=html} 
toyBioc/├── DESCRIPTION├── NAMESPACE├── NEWS.md├── README.md├── R/├── man/├── tests/│   ├── testthat.R│   └── testthat/├── src/  (optional)├── data/├── inst/│   ├── extdata/│   └── scripts/└── vignettes/
  • DESCRIPTION: metadata
  • NAMESPACE: what's imported and exported
  • R/: R code
  • man/: documentation (generated by roxygen2)
  • tests/: unit tests
  • src/: compiled code (C/C++, Rust), optional
  • data/: R objects (.rda) for examples
  • inst/: files installed as they are
  • vignettes/: long-form documentation
  • README.md, NEWS.md: other files
``` ## tests/: write tests right after the code Tests check if your functions work as expected, and should be written early. ```r usethis::use_r("normalizeCounts") # 1. write the function in R/ usethis::use_test("normalizeCounts") # 2. write its tests, right away devtools::load_all() # 3. load the package... devtools::test() # ...run the tests, and repeat ``` . . . Advantages of writing tests early: - You still remember the **edge cases** you had in mind while writing the code - Bugs are caught **early**, when they're easy to fix - You can **refactor** later with confidence: tests tell you if you broke something - Tests **document** how the function is supposed to behave ## tests/: writing unit tests with {testthat} ```r usethis::use_testthat() # tests/testthat.R + tests/testthat/ usethis::use_test("normalizeCounts") # tests/testthat/test-normalizeCounts.R ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r ## Toy data: 3 genes x 2 samples counts <- matrix(c(10, 0, 5, 20, 3, 7), nrow = 3) test_that("normalizeCounts() returns CPM values", { cpm <- normalizeCounts(counts, method = "cpm") expect_true(is.matrix(cpm)) expect_equal(dim(cpm), dim(counts)) expect_equal(unname(colSums(cpm)), c(1e6, 1e6)) }) test_that("normalizeCounts() throws errors for invalid input", { expect_error(normalizeCounts(as.data.frame(counts)), "numeric matrix") expect_error(normalizeCounts(-counts), "negative") }) ``` ::: ::: ## tests/: how much of my code is tested? ```{.r .cell-code} cov <- covr::package_coverage(toy_path) cat(render_coverage_html(cov, toy_path, from_line = 17)) ```

The lines in red have **never been executed** by the tests: the `"log2cpm"` option and the warning for `NA`s. ::: ## tests/: covering all lines Add tests for **every option** of each argument and **every error or warning** your code can raise: ```r test_that("normalizeCounts() returns log2-CPM values", { lcpm <- normalizeCounts(counts, method = "log2cpm") expect_equal(lcpm, log2(normalizeCounts(counts) + 1)) }) test_that("normalizeCounts() warns about NAs", { counts_na <- counts counts_na[1, 1] <- NA expect_warning(normalizeCounts(counts_na), "NA values") }) ``` - Test **edge cases**: `NA`s, empty inputs, a single sample, all zeros - Simulate failures, e.g., a file that doesn't exist or invalid input - Look at coverage interactively with `covr::report()` ## tests/: good testing practices **Use toy data sets** - Small objects created in the test file or in `tests/testthat/helper-*.R` - Or small example data that ships with the package (`data/`, `inst/extdata/`) - Tests should run in **seconds** . . . **Avoid over-testing** - Test **behaviour** (inputs → outputs), not implementation details - Don't test other packages' functions - Avoid many near-duplicate tests - 100% coverage is not a goal in itself ## Package structure: src/ {.anatomy-slide} ```{=html} 
toyBioc/├── DESCRIPTION├── NAMESPACE├── NEWS.md├── README.md├── R/├── man/├── tests/│   ├── testthat.R│   └── testthat/├── src/  (optional)├── data/├── inst/│   ├── extdata/│   └── scripts/└── vignettes/
  • DESCRIPTION: metadata
  • NAMESPACE: what's imported and exported
  • R/: R code
  • man/: documentation (generated by roxygen2)
  • tests/: unit tests
  • src/: compiled code (C/C++, Rust), optional
  • data/: R objects (.rda) for examples
  • inst/: files installed as they are
  • vignettes/: long-form documentation
  • README.md, NEWS.md: other files
``` ## src/: do you really need it? `src/` is **optional**. Most Bioconductor packages are written in pure R. Cost of compiled code: - Users (and Bioconductor's build machines) need **compilers** and system libraries on Linux, macOS and Windows - Builds can fail on one platform only, and memory errors (segfaults) are **hard to debug** - Fewer people can **review**, contribute to, and maintain the code ## src/: do you really need it? (cont'd) Only add compiled code in the (rare) cases where **well-written R code is still too slow**, and you have **measured** that it is. The workflow: 1. Write correct R code, with tests 2. **Profile** it to find the bottleneck 3. Optimise the bottleneck in R, and **benchmark** the alternatives 4. Still too slow? Only then rewrite that bottleneck in C++ or Rust ## Profile first: where is the time spent? Profiling code with [profvis](https://profvis.r-lib.org/). ```r library(profvis) profvis({ counts <- simulateCounts(n_genes = 20000, n_samples = 50) cpm <- normalizeCounts(counts, method = "log2cpm") res <- testDifferentialExpression(cpm, condition) }) ``` profvis opens an interactive flame graph showing how much **time** and **memory** each line takes. . . . - Usually, a **single function or loop** is responsible for most of the run time - Optimise **that** part only. ## Benchmark: compare alternatives Once you've found the bottleneck, compare alternative implementations with [bench](https://bench.r-lib.org/): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- matrix(rnorm(1e5 * 10), ncol = 10) # 100,000 genes x 10 samples colSumsLoop <- function(x) { out <- c() for (j in seq_len(ncol(x))) { s <- 0 for (i in seq_len(nrow(x))) s <- s + x[i, j] out <- c(out, s) } out } bench::mark( loop = colSumsLoop(m), apply = apply(m, 2, sum), colSums = colSums(m), iterations = 20 )[, c("expression", "min", "median", "mem_alloc")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> # A tibble: 3 × 4 #> expression min median mem_alloc #> #> 1 loop 16.5ms 16.65ms 36.5KB #> 2 apply 7.44ms 7.73ms 19.1MB #> 3 colSums 651.41µs 690.02µs 0B ``` ::: ::: ## src/: C++ code with Rcpp For bottlenecks that can't be solved in R, write C++ code with [Rcpp](https://www.rcpp.org/): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Rcpp::cppFunction(" NumericVector colSumsCpp(NumericMatrix x) { int nc = x.ncol(); NumericVector out(nc); for (int j = 0; j < nc; j++) { out[j] = sum(x(_, j)); } return out; }") colSumsCpp(matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 3 7 11 ``` ::: ::: ## src/: was it worth it? Always benchmark your compiled code against the **best R version**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res <- bench::mark(R = colSums(m), Rcpp = colSumsCpp(m), iterations = 50) res[, c("expression", "min", "median", "mem_alloc")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> # A tibble: 2 × 4 #> expression min median mem_alloc #> #> 1 R 648.1µs 706.78µs 0B #> 2 Rcpp 1.51ms 1.58ms 5.17KB ``` ::: ::: ## src/: Rcpp inside a package ```r usethis::use_rcpp() # creates src/, adds Rcpp to LinkingTo and Imports ``` :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} `src/colsums.cpp` ```cpp #include using namespace Rcpp; // [[Rcpp::export]] NumericVector colSumsCpp(NumericMatrix x) { ... } ``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} `R/toyBioc-package.R` ```r #' @useDynLib toyBioc, .registration = TRUE #' @importFrom Rcpp sourceCpp NULL ``` Then `devtools::document()` runs `Rcpp::compileAttributes()`, which creates `R/RcppExports.R` and `src/RcppExports.cpp`. ::: :::: ## src/: Rust code with rextendr [rextendr](https://extendr.github.io/rextendr/) does for Rust what Rcpp does for C++. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="45%"} ```r ## Set up Rust in the package rextendr::use_extendr() ## After editing src/rust/src/lib.rs rextendr::document() ``` ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ```rust use extendr_api::prelude::*; /// @export #[extendr] fn hello_rust() -> &'static str { "Hello from Rust!" } extendr_module! { mod toyBioc; fn hello_rust; } ``` ::: :::: Add `SystemRequirements: Cargo (Rust's package manager), rustc` to DESCRIPTION ## Package structure: data/ {.anatomy-slide} ```{=html} 
toyBioc/├── DESCRIPTION├── NAMESPACE├── NEWS.md├── README.md├── R/├── man/├── tests/│   ├── testthat.R│   └── testthat/├── src/  (optional)├── data/├── inst/│   ├── extdata/│   └── scripts/└── vignettes/
  • DESCRIPTION: metadata
  • NAMESPACE: what's imported and exported
  • R/: R code
  • man/: documentation (generated by roxygen2)
  • tests/: unit tests
  • src/: compiled code (C/C++, Rust), optional
  • data/: R objects (.rda) for examples
  • inst/: files installed as they are
  • vignettes/: long-form documentation
  • README.md, NEWS.md: other files
``` ## data/: R objects for examples ```r ## Save an object to data/ (code to create it goes in inst/scripts/) usethis::use_data(example_counts) ``` Document data sets in `R/data.R`: ```r #' Example RNA-seq count matrix #' #' Simulated counts for 6 genes and 4 samples (2 controls, 2 treated). #' #' @format A numeric matrix with 6 rows (genes) and 4 columns (samples). #' @source Simulated with `inst/scripts/make-counts.R`. #' @usage data(example_counts) "example_counts" ``` - **Keep data small**: the package tarball must be **< 10 MB**, and each file **≤ 5 MB** - For larger data, use **ExperimentHub** or an experiment data package ## Package structure: inst/ {.anatomy-slide} ```{=html} 
toyBioc/├── DESCRIPTION├── NAMESPACE├── NEWS.md├── README.md├── R/├── man/├── tests/│   ├── testthat.R│   └── testthat/├── src/  (optional)├── data/├── inst/│   ├── extdata/│   └── scripts/└── vignettes/
  • DESCRIPTION: metadata
  • NAMESPACE: what's imported and exported
  • R/: R code
  • man/: documentation (generated by roxygen2)
  • tests/: unit tests
  • src/: compiled code (C/C++, Rust), optional
  • data/: R objects (.rda) for examples
  • inst/: files installed as they are
  • vignettes/: long-form documentation
  • README.md, NEWS.md: other files
``` ## inst/extdata and inst/scripts Files in `inst/` are installed as they are. Raw files (e.g., `.tsv`, `.bam`, `.fasta`) go in `inst/extdata/`. You can find them with `system.file()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counts_file <- system.file("extdata", "counts.tsv", package = "toyBioc") counts <- as.matrix(read.delim(counts_file, row.names = 1)) head(counts, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> ctrl1 ctrl2 trt1 trt2 #> gene1 89 90 82 65 #> gene2 50 121 98 68 #> gene3 160 63 123 102 ``` ::: ::: . . . **Document how each file was created** in `inst/scripts/` (data source, URL, filtering, code), so users can roughly reproduce it. ## Package structure: vignettes/ {.anatomy-slide} ```{=html} 
toyBioc/├── DESCRIPTION├── NAMESPACE├── NEWS.md├── README.md├── R/├── man/├── tests/│   ├── testthat.R│   └── testthat/├── src/  (optional)├── data/├── inst/│   ├── extdata/│   └── scripts/└── vignettes/
  • DESCRIPTION: metadata
  • NAMESPACE: what's imported and exported
  • R/: R code
  • man/: documentation (generated by roxygen2)
  • tests/: unit tests
  • src/: compiled code (C/C++, Rust), optional
  • data/: R objects (.rda) for examples
  • inst/: files installed as they are
  • vignettes/: long-form documentation
  • README.md, NEWS.md: other files
``` ## vignettes/: long-form documentation At least one vignette (`.Rmd` or `.qmd`) with **executed** code, using `BiocStyle::html_document`. Start from `biocthis::use_bioc_vignette()`. Expected sections: 1. **Introduction**: motivation, what the package does, and how it compares with other Bioconductor packages 2. **Installation**: in a chunk that isn't evaluated ```r if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager") BiocManager::install("toyBioc") ``` 3. **Usage (or multiple sections)**: worked examples 4. **Session information**: `sessionInfo()` at the end 5. **References** ## Vignettes: do's and don'ts :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.bad} ````markdown ## Normalization ```{{r}} cpm <- normalizeCounts(counts) ``` ```{{r, eval=FALSE}} res <- runAnalysis(big_dataset) ``` ```` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.good} ````markdown ## Normalization Library sizes differ across samples, so raw counts can't be compared directly. Here, we normalize them to counts per million (CPM): ```{{r}} cpm <- normalizeCounts(counts) colSums(cpm) ``` All columns now sum to 1 million, so expression levels are comparable across samples. ```` ::: ::: :::: ## Vignettes: a vignette is teaching material - Put **text before and after every chunk**: what is the code going to do? How should the output be interpreted? - **Execute all chunks**. Static vignettes (`eval = FALSE` everywhere) are not accepted - Use **small example data**. The goal is to show how to use the package, not to reproduce a paper's results - **Don't assume prior knowledge**: explain the data, the classes and the biology - Show a **complete workflow** that users can copy and adapt ## Package structure: other files {.anatomy-slide} ```{=html} 
toyBioc/├── DESCRIPTION├── NAMESPACE├── NEWS.md├── README.md├── R/├── man/├── tests/│   ├── testthat.R│   └── testthat/├── src/  (optional)├── data/├── inst/│   ├── extdata/│   └── scripts/└── vignettes/
  • DESCRIPTION: metadata
  • NAMESPACE: what's imported and exported
  • R/: R code
  • man/: documentation (generated by roxygen2)
  • tests/: unit tests
  • src/: compiled code (C/C++, Rust), optional
  • data/: R objects (.rda) for examples
  • inst/: files installed as they are
  • vignettes/: long-form documentation
  • README.md, NEWS.md: other files
``` ## Other files - `README.md`: shown on GitHub. Say what the package does and how to install it - `NEWS.md`: what changed in each version (shown on the landing page) - `inst/CITATION`: how to cite your package (e.g., the paper) # Checking and submitting {background-color="#1a81c2"} ## R CMD check vs BiocCheck | | `R CMD check` | `BiocCheck` | |-|---------------|-------------| | **Check** | R package requirements: installs, examples run, tests pass, docs match code, ... | Bioconductor guidelines: biocViews, version number, vignette, coding practices, formatting, ... | | **Run with** | `devtools::check()` | `BiocCheck::BiocCheck()` | | **Examples of issues** | Undocumented arguments, undeclared dependencies, failing tests | `sapply()`, `1:n`, lines > 80 chars, `\dontrun{}`, missing `sessionInfo()` in vignette | : {.smaller tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"} . . . Your package must pass `R CMD check` and `BiocCheck` with **0 errors and 0 warnings**. Fix NOTEs too, or justify them to the reviewer. ## Running the checks ```r ## In the package directory devtools::check() # R CMD build + R CMD check ## On the package source BiocCheck::BiocCheck() ```
Limits to keep in mind: - `R CMD check` must take **less than 10 minutes** - Package tarball **< 10 MB**. Individual files **≤ 5 MB** - Vignettes, examples and tests should use **< 8 GB** of memory - Develop and test with the **devel** version of Bioconductor ## The submission process Since 2026, submissions go through [Bioconductor/BiocContributions](https://github.com/Bioconductor/BiocContributions), with builds and checks run by **rOpenSci's R-universe** (GitHub Actions). ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| fig-width: 11 flowchart LR A["Open an issue at
BiocContributions"] --> B["Automatic
precheck"] B --> C["Accept policies
(/accept-policies)"] C --> D["Builds on R-universe
(R CMD check,
BiocCheck)"] D --> E["Review
in progress"] E --> F["Package
accepted"] E --> G["Package
declined"] style F fill:#2e8540,color:#fff style G fill:#c0392b,color:#fff ``` Each step is shown as a **label** on your GitHub issue (*precheck-passed*, *pre-review*, *Build OK* / *Build Error*, *review in progress*, *package accepted*, ...). ## Submitting, step by step 1. Put your package in a **public GitHub repository** named exactly like the package 2. Open an issue at [BiocContributions](https://github.com/Bioconductor/BiocContributions) using the **new submission template**, with your repository's URL 3. An **automatic precheck** looks at `DESCRIPTION` (version `x.99.y`, `biocViews`, no `Remotes:`), `vignettes/` and file sizes 4. Read the policies posted in the issue and comment **`/accept-policies`** 5. Your repository is copied to the **BiocStaging** organisation and added to an R-universe. **From now on, push changes there** 6. **Bump the version** (`0.99.0` → `0.99.1`) with each push to trigger a new build. Build reports are posted in the issue ## The review - A **reviewer** is assigned once there are no build ERRORs (justify any remaining WARNINGs or NOTEs in a comment). Label: *review in progress* - Reviewers are **volunteers** who go through your code, docs and vignette against the guidelines - Reviews usually start **within ~3 weeks** of a clean build, and may take several rounds - If a review stalls and you don't reply, the package may be marked as *inactive review* and the issue closed ## The review (cont'd) Tips: - **Respond to every comment** in the issue, point by point (what you changed, or why you didn't) - Push all fixes (with a version bump), then comment on the issue - Think of it as **free code review from experienced developers**. # Maintaining a package {background-color="#1a81c2"} ## After acceptance - Your package is moved to **Bioconductor devel**, and you get a **BiocCredentials** account to manage the SSH keys for push access - It goes into the next **release** (April or October) - Each release creates a **release branch** (bug fixes only) and you keep developing on **devel** (new features) - Version numbers: `x.y.z`, with **even `y`** in release and **odd `y`** in devel (e.g., `1.2.0` in release, `1.3.0` in devel). **Bump `z`** with every change you push ::: {.mermaid-short} ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| fig-width: 10 flowchart LR A["Submission
versions 0.99.z"] -- accepted --> R(("Bioc
release")) R --> B["devel branch
1.1.z: new features"] R --> C["RELEASE_3_23 branch
1.0.z: bug fixes only"] style B fill:#1a81c2,color:#fff style C fill:#87b13f,color:#fff ``` ::: ## Being a maintainer - Check the **nightly build reports** and fix errors and warnings quickly (failures are sent from `BBS-noreply@bioconductor.org`) - Answer questions on the [support site](https://support.bioconductor.org/) (add your package to your *Watched Tags*) - Subscribe to the **bioc-devel** mailing list - Keep the maintainer email in DESCRIPTION up to date - To remove functions, follow the **deprecation guidelines** (`.Deprecated()` → `.Defunct()` across releases) # Wrapping up {background-color="#1a81c2"} ## Checklist before submitting :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} - [ ] In scope, with ≥ 2 biocViews leaf terms - [ ] Reuses Bioconductor classes - [ ] Informative `Description` (≥ 3 sentences) - [ ] Open license - [ ] Few dependencies, with niche ones in `Suggests` - [ ] `@importFrom`, not `@import` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} - [ ] Every exported function documented, with types and examples - [ ] Unit tests covering all options and errors - [ ] Small data, with provenance in `inst/scripts/` - [ ] Executed vignette that teaches - [ ] `R CMD check` and `BiocCheck`: 0 errors, 0 warnings ::: :::: ## Resources - 📖 [Bioconductor Contributions Guide](https://contributions.bioconductor.org/): package guidelines and the review process - 📖 [*R Packages* (2e)](https://r-pkgs.org/): Wickham & Bryan - 📦 [biocthis](https://lcolladotor.github.io/biocthis/): templates for Bioconductor packages - 📝 [BiocContributions](https://github.com/Bioconductor/BiocContributions): where packages are submitted (see `docs/submitters.md`) - 💬 [Support site](https://support.bioconductor.org/) and [Bioconductor Zulip chat](https://chat.bioconductor.org/) (e.g., the *#package-submission* channel) ## Thank you! {.center} ::: {.r-fit-text} Questions? :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
